nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Stone Crab
Scientific Name: Menippe mercenaria

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Arthropoda
	Class: Malacostraca
	Order: Decapoda
	Family: Xanthidae

Note: 	Subphylum: Crustacea

Other Common Names: Florida Stone Crab


Synonymy: Cancer mercenaria Say, 1818
Phylogeny: Menippe mercenaria has recently undergone systematic revision and was split into M. mercenaria and M. adina. Menippe adinia dwells along the western and northern portions of the Gulf of Mexico. It is assumed here that much of the biology will be similar between the species and only slight differences in seasonal matings, spawnings, habitats and behaviors may occur. It will take some time before these differences can be ascertained in the field and laboratory. Microhabitat distinctions between the species appears to occur. M. adina occurs both sub- and intertidally, whereas M. mercenaria is intertidal only in the hybrid zone (764).

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (768)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  The commercial importance of stone crabs comes from the meat of their chela and appears to be a relatively local phenomenon. The south of Florida is the major area of commercial importance with most of the crab claws being consumed in that same area without export. The same appears to be true of south Texas estuaries and fisherman. Although some from Texas are transported to the increased demand of Florida (Mark Tobb, per. comm. )

Within Study Area: Common through out the northern Gulf of Mexico with concentrated areas in south Texas estuaries.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall: Wakulla County, Florida, west and south around Gulf of Mexico to Tamaulipas State, Mexico (768) .

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs: are maintained by the female beneath her abdomen until hatching.
Larvae: are planktonic.
Adults: and juveniles are demersal, with adults often forming deep burrows in mud sediments. Juveniles usually do not form burrows, but use readily available crevices in close proximity to food.

Stone crabs have often been suggested as being nocturnal, however there is equal activity at mid day and mid night which suggests a crepuscular activity cycle.  Minor movements by the females from grass flats to deeper waters to avoid extreme temperatures have been noted, while males move from offshore areas to the grass flats for mating.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Marine to estuarine for all life stages.

Substrate: Stone crabs are found in seagrass and mud flats to rock jetties. Adults borrow under rock ledges, coral heads and dead shell or grass clumps (FMP).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Stone crabs in general can tolerate waters ranging from 8-32 C, in cooler temperatures they often seal their burrows with mud (569). Larvae do not tolerate temperatures below 20 C, only being able to develop to the megalopae stage (522).

Salinity: Ong and Costlow (522) found larvae have low survival rates at low salinities (20-25 ppt) at 20 C; and did not survive in a salinity of 10 ppt. Adults are considered euryhaline although they are usually found in salinities close to seawater.

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, diecious; copulation usually takes place within a burrow or crevice. Mating is usually from November to March, sequenced with the spawning season (March to November, or possibly throughout the year in warmer climates).

Mating/Spawning: Sperm are stored by the female in the seminal receptacle, only a portion of the sperm are used at a spawning period, some maintained for later spawns. A female can spawn up to six times before mating again. Wilbur (764) observed a maximum number of five clutches carried by a single female in a 93 d period. Males will guard the females for longer periods after females molt if another male stone crab is present, and after copulation (765).

Fecundity: A single female can produce between 4-6 egg masses during a spawning season, averaging 4.5 spawnings per molt (111). Each sponge may contain 0.5-1.0 million eggs. Growth and Development Egg: Fertilized eggs are maintained by the female until hatching usually a period of 9-14 days.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Larvae: Fastest growth was achieved in the laboratory at 30 C and 30-35 ppt, in which the megalopae stage was reached in 14 days and first crab stage in 21 days (522).  megalops, zoea

Juvenile: Juvenile growth is expected to cover 7 molts in 320 days and has intermolts of 40 days increasing in 15 % increments per molt.  1.4-30 mm CW

Adult: Males are heavier and gain weight faster than females (687). Terminal molts has been suggested to occur around 112 rnm CW; while others have reached sizes of 130-145 mrn CW.  30-35+ Carapace Width (CW)

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body:
Stone crabs appear to be entirely carnivorous at all stages of their lives.
Larvae: generally consume zooplankton.
Juvenile: diets are unknown; while those in captivity ate small bivalves, oyster drills, beef liver and chicken parts, polychaetes and each other.
Adult: use their heavy chelae to crush all types of mollusks.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Menippe mercenaria has recently undergone systematic revision. The species that dwells along the western and northern portions of the Gulf of Mexico has attained species recognition and goes by the name Menippe adinia. It is assumed here that much of the biology will be similar between the species and only slight differences in seasonal matings, spawnings, habitats and behaviors may occur. It will take some time before  these differences can be ascertained in the field and laboratory. Microhabitat distinctions between the species can be made. M. adina occurs both sub- and intertidally, whereas M. mercenaria is intertidal only in the hybrid zone (764). The Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council's Scientific and Statistical Committee recently (May 1990) defined overfishing of stone crabs as occurring when crab claws are harvested at a size when the number of eggslrecruit is reduced below 70%. The fishery is well above the 70% level at present.

nodes.title: PEOPLE CONSULTED
nodes.body: Mark Tobb; Lu Belle's Seafood Brokerage, Port Aransas, Texas

Salinity: Ong and Costlow (522) found larvae have low survival rates at low salinities (20-25 ppt) at 20 C; and did not survive in a salinity of 10 ppt. Adults are considered euryhaline although they are usually found in salinities close to seawater.

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode: Sexual, diecious; copulation usually takes place within a burrow or crevice. Mating is usually from November to March, sequenced with the spawning season (March to November, or possibly throughout the year in warmer climates).

Mating/Spawning: Sperm are stored by the female in the seminal receptacle, only a portion of the sperm are used at a spawning period, some maintained for later spawns. A female can spawn up to six times before mating again. Wilbur (764) observed a maximum number of five clutches carried by a single female in a 93 d period. Males will guard the females for longer periods after females molt if another male stone crab is present, and after copulation (765).

Fecundity: A single female can produce between 4-6 egg masses during a spawning season, averaging 4.5 spawnings per molt (111). Each sponge may contain 0.5-1.0 million eggs. Growth and Development Egg: Fertilized eggs are maintained by the female until hatching usually a period of 9-14 days.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Larvae: Fastest growth was achieved in the laboratory at 30 C and 30-35 ppt, in which the megalopae stage was reached in 14 days and first crab stage in 21 days (522).  megalops, zoea

Juvenile: Juvenile growth is expected to cover 7 molts in 320 days and has intermolts of 40 days increasing in 15 % increments per molt.  1.4-30 mm CW

Adult: Males are heavier and gain weight faster than females (687). Terminal molts has been suggested to occur around 112 rnm CW; while others have reached sizes of 130-145 mrn CW.  30-35+ Carapace Width (CW)

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content:
Stone crabs appear to be entirely carnivorous at all stages of their lives.
Larvae: generally consume zooplankton.
Juvenile: diets are unknown; while those in captivity ate small bivalves, oyster drills, beef liver and chicken parts, polychaetes and each other.
Adult: use their heavy chelae to crush all types of mollusks.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Menippe mercenaria has recently undergone systematic revision. The species that dwells along the western and northern portions of the Gulf of Mexico has attained species recognition and goes by the name Menippe adinia. It is assumed here that much of the biology will be similar between the species and only slight differences in seasonal matings, spawnings, habitats and behaviors may occur. It will take some time before  these differences can be ascertained in the field and laboratory. Microhabitat distinctions between the species can be made. M. adina occurs both sub- and intertidally, whereas M. mercenaria is intertidal only in the hybrid zone (764). The Gulf of Mexico Fishery Management Council's Scientific and Statistical Committee recently (May 1990) defined overfishing of stone crabs as occurring when crab claws are harvested at a size when the number of eggslrecruit is reduced below 70%. The fishery is well above the 70% level at present.
